recent_posts.title: Building an 8-node NVIDIA GB10 cluster for local LLM inference
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on walkthrough of building an 8-node NVIDIA GB10 cluster with 1TB of unified memory for running large local AI models like Kimi K2.5/K2.6 and Qwen 3.5 397B. The setup uses 200Gbps RDMA networking via MikroTik CRS804 switches, a Ubiquiti 10GbE management network, and shared NAS storage. A key highlight is that AI coding agents (Claude Code, OpenClaude) were used to handle the entire cluster configuration — RDMA tuning, RoCEv2 QoS, VLM deployment, and documentation — with minimal manual intervention. Performance framing focuses on model quality and flexibility rather than raw tokens/second, with the cluster running at ~950W under load. Cost comparison against Apple Mac Studio M3 Ultra alternatives is discussed, with the GB10 cluster totaling ~$23K for ~1TB of memory.

recent_posts.title: Ace Magic M1A Pro Plus 128GB AMD Strix Halo mini PC review
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on review of the Ace Magic M1A Pro Plus, a tank-styled mini PC featuring the AMD Ryzen AI Max Plus 395 (Zen 5, 16-core), 128GB unified memory, and AMD Radeon 860S GPU. The system targets local AI workloads and light gaming, priced well above $2,000. Notable features include a physical RGB dial for switching between 70W/100W/140W TDP profiles on the fly, easy-access side panels for NVMe SSDs, dual 2.5GbE ports with Wi-Fi 7, and three display outputs plus a front USB-C. Compared to Nvidia GB10 systems, it offers lower cost and better Windows compatibility but less scalability. The reviewer recommends running large models slowly over smaller quantized models for agentic AI workflows, and notes a pre-production SSD slot stability bug that Ace Magic says is fixed in retail units.

recent_posts.title: How AI and compute are used inside retail stores
recent_posts.summary: A walkthrough of how AI and compute are used throughout retail environments, filmed inside an Ace Hardware store. Covers use cases including parking lot traffic analytics, in-store heat maps, shelf monitoring, shoplifting detection, spill detection, digital price tags, self-checkout verification, employee effectiveness monitoring, and back-end data center analytics. Notes that much retail AI inference runs on CPUs (like AMD EPYC) rather than GPUs, and traces the evolution from manual processes to computerized and AI-enhanced workflows across customer, employee, and operator experiences.

recent_posts.title: Using an AI agent to autonomously configure a ZFS NAS and Proxmox homelab
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on experiment where an AI coding agent (OpenClaw/Claude) is given SSH root access to a Beink ME Pro mini PC NAS and tasked with fully configuring it as a homelab node. The AI autonomously set up Proxmox VE, configured ZFS RAID-1 with two 28TB drives, deployed LXC containers, installed Tailscale VPN, Uptime Kuma, and Nginx Proxy Manager — all within a couple of hours using local LLMs (Minimax M2.5, Qwen 3) running on Apple Silicon and AMD hardware. The hardware itself is reviewed: Intel N95 quad-core, 12GB LPDDR5, dual 2.5G/5G Ethernet, three M.2 slots (PCIe Gen 3 only). Key takeaways include the impressive capability of AI agents for sysadmin tasks, the security risks of granting root SSH access, and the implication that homelab setup no longer requires deep IT skills.

recent_posts.title: Inside a Supermicro NVIDIA B300 AI factory hardware tour
recent_posts.summary: A sponsored tour of Supermicro's AI server lineup in San Jose, covering the full stack of components needed to build modern AI factories. The walkthrough covers NVIDIA HGX B200 vs B300 8-GPU platforms highlighting the shift from ConnectX-7 (400Gbps) to ConnectX-8 (800Gbps) networking now integrated into the baseboard, the GB300 NVL72 rack with 72 Blackwell GPUs and Grace CPUs, ORV3 form factor systems enabling up to 144 GPUs per 48U rack, liquid cooling infrastructure including cold plates, rack manifolds, in-row CDUs, rear door heat exchangers, liquid-to-air sidecars, and outdoor cooling towers. The software stack (SuperCloud Composer, Automation Center, Director, Developer Console) is also covered, showing how Supermicro positions itself as a full-stack AI infrastructure provider from silicon to facility cooling.

recent_posts.title: Minisforum MS-02 Ultra review for homelab and NAS use cases
recent_posts.summary: A detailed hardware review of the Minisforum MS-02 Ultra mini PC, covering its 24-core Intel Core Ultra 9 285HX CPU, 62.5 Gbps total networking (two 25GbE SFP28 ports via Intel E810, one 10GbE, one 2.5GbE), three PCIe expansion slots, multiple M.2 SSD slots, USB4 v2 ports, internal power supply, and optional ECC memory support. The review covers internal layout, PCIe bifurcation details, power consumption (idle ~20W, sustained load ~145W), noise levels (~36-41 dBA under load), and practical use cases including homelab virtualization, NAS, AI inference, and desktop use. Key caveats include no hyperthreading on the CPU, PCIe slot lane limitations (3x4 not x16), and thermal constraints for high-power expansion cards.

recent_posts.title: Server buying strategies for 2026 amid rising DRAM and NAND prices
recent_posts.summary: With DRAM and NAND pricing rising sharply in 2026, server buyers need smarter purchasing strategies. Five key recommendations are covered: buy early before prices rise further, rethink single-socket vs dual-socket node strategy (single-socket now offers up to 192 cores and can match dual-socket DIMM counts), optimize software licensing costs by choosing frequency-optimized CPUs like AMD EPYC 9575F that replace far more old Xeon cores, be strategic about DIMM population and memory clock speeds to balance cost and performance, and stop wasting money on over-provisioned or poorly matched configurations. KVM virtualization is recommended over bare-metal low-end boxes to avoid VMware licensing costs. New CPU generations (AMD EPYC Venice, Intel Xeon Diamond Rapids 16-channel) are coming later in 2026, so buyers should weigh whether to buy current-gen now at locked-in prices or wait for next-gen platforms.

recent_posts.title: Testing MikroTik's NEW All-in-One WiFi, PoE Switch, Router
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on hardware review of the MikroTik CRS418PG-2S+RM, a 1U rack-mount all-in-one switch featuring 16x 1GbE ports (8 with PoE+, 150W budget), 2x SFP+ 10G uplinks, Wi-Fi 6 4x4 MIMO (on the Wi-Fi variant), redundant internal power supplies, a Qualcomm IPQ8724 quad-core ARM CPU enabling basic routing, and a USB 3 port. Performance testing using professional Keysight IXIA gear revealed minor frame loss at 100% line rate with 64-byte packets — a finding confirmed by MikroTik, who allow a 0.1% variance in their own specs. Routing throughput reaches roughly 2.5 Gbps bidirectional for HTTP traffic. Priced under $500, it suits small deployments needing an integrated wired/wireless/PoE solution, though the reviewer notes the 1GbE limitation and wishes for 2.5GbE and Wi-Fi 7 in a future revision.

recent_posts.title: Even an NVIDIA GPU and 3x SSDs fit in 1L Lenovo ThinkStation P3 Tiny Gen2
recent_posts.summary: The Lenovo ThinkStation P3 Tiny Gen2 packs a 24-core Intel Core Ultra 9 285 processor, NVIDIA RTX A1000 GPU with 8GB memory, up to three M.2 SSDs, and Wi-Fi 7 into a 1-liter chassis. The system features extensive USB connectivity (mostly Type-A), 1GbE with Intel vPro, and easy tool-free serviceability. Power consumption ranges from 29-46W idle to ~185-240W under load, with noise levels reaching 45dBA at full load. While more expensive than budget mini PCs, it offers enterprise-grade support, extensive configuration options, and significantly more compute resources than older generation 1L systems.

recent_posts.title: Sedola 12 port 10GbE switch review and performance testing
recent_posts.summary: The Sedola SLSWTG W2C48NS is a budget 10GbE switch offering 12 ports (8 SFP+ and 4 10GBASE-T) for around $200-230. Performance testing using professional EX network hardware and RFC 2544 methodology shows the Realtek RTL9313-based switch handles full line-rate traffic without packet loss, even during extended 20-hour tests. While it includes a fan that produces 37-38 dBA with a pulsating noise pattern and basic web management, it delivers exceptional value by combining the functionality of separate 4-port 10GBASE-T and 8-port SFP+ switches at a fraction of the combined cost. Power consumption sits at 13W idle, jumping to 14.6W with active 10GBASE-T ports.
